challenges.headline: 'Edit the total' is undefined
challenges.premise: The request treats editing a reported total as a simple field change.
challenges.alternative: Treating the edit as a traceable adjustment entry — a new, attributed, reversible line that makes the total add up — keeps the report reconcilable with its source data; an outright override does not.
challenges.consequence: Without this decision, the build defaults to whichever is easier to code, and an override with no visible marker is exactly how a financial report quietly stops tying back to its own data — a compliance and trust failure, not just a bug.
challenges.recommendation: Get Finance to explicitly choose adjustment-entry vs. override before any schema work starts; this decision shapes the data model, not just a UI label.

challenges.headline: Closed-period editing left open
challenges.premise: Nothing in the request addresses whether a total can still be edited once its period has been reviewed and closed.
challenges.alternative: Locking closed periods and routing corrections through an adjustment in the next open period preserves what was already filed or exported, instead of silently rewriting history.
challenges.consequence: If closed-period edits are allowed by default, every prior export or filed report built from that period becomes retroactively wrong with no record of the change — a direct audit exposure in a domain where auditability is explicitly regulated.
challenges.recommendation: Define the period lifecycle and lock rule before building the edit feature — this determines whether 'edit' and 'close' are even the same code path.

challenges.headline: Export treated as a file, not a contract
challenges.premise: The request describes exporting figures 'for the finance team' as if it were a simple download.
challenges.alternative: Defining the export as a versioned, reproducible snapshot with an agreed schema and destination protects against silent rejects downstream and lets a previously sent export be retrieved exactly as sent, even after the underlying figures change.
challenges.consequence: Without this, a later correction to a total invalidates every export already sent, with no way to tell which version a consumer acted on — and if the destination is an accounting system, an unspecified schema risks a rejected file discovered late.
challenges.recommendation: Identify the export's actual consumer and required format now, and decide whether exports must be retained as immutable snapshots.

The adjustment-entry pattern (a new, attributed, reversible line correcting a derived total) mirrors how Invoicing handles credit notes against issued invoices — worth designing as a shared 'correction entry' concept rather than two bespoke mechanisms.

The versioned, retained export snapshot is structurally similar to how a signed Contract version stays referenceable after supersession — a generalized 'immutable artifact' abstraction could serve both.

decisions.alternative: Ship the edit feature first and add logging later if requested.
decisions.tradeoff: More upfront engineering effort now, in exchange for avoiding a costly retrofit and a compliance gap if an audit occurs before logging is added.

challenges.headline: 'Edit the total' as a direct write
challenges.premise: The request treats editing a reported total like editing any field — set a new value and save.
challenges.alternative: Model the correction as an adjustment entry: a new, attributed, reversible line that makes the total add up, leaving the original entries untouched and visible.
challenges.consequence: A direct override replaces the derived value and silently disagrees with its own source data — the report stops tying out, and that's usually discovered at audit time, not at build time.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with Finance whether corrections must remain traceable to source entries before deciding the edit mechanism.

challenges.headline: Export as a simple deliverable
challenges.premise: The request implies exporting figures 'for the finance team' is a one-off file action.
challenges.alternative: Treat the export as a contract with a specific downstream consumer (accounting system, filing package, spreadsheet) — with an agreed schema, rounding convention, and versioned retention so a past export stays reproducible.
challenges.consequence: Building a generic export first risks a rebuild once the real consumer and format surface, and an unversioned export can't be reproduced if the underlying figures later change.
challenges.recommendation: Identify the actual downstream consumer and its schema requirements before implementing the export.

challenges.headline: Undifferentiated 'users' editing figures
challenges.premise: The request refers to 'users' editing totals and 'the finance team' receiving exports, without distinguishing who may adjust, approve, or close.
challenges.alternative: Define separate roles for adjuster, approver, and period-closer, matching the segregation-of-duties expectation already standard in this domain.
challenges.consequence: Letting the same role adjust and close a period is a textbook audit finding, and retrofitting role separation after permissions are wired in is expensive.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the role model and segregation rules with Finance before building the permission layer.
